title: Why God Waited for Joseph
paragraphs:
Why God Waited for Joseph
The Years That Felt Like Abandonment Were Actually Preparation—And What God Is Doing in Your Delay Right Now
There is a kind of pain that only comes from waiting.
Not the waiting in a grocery line.
Not the waiting for a text message.
Not even the waiting for a breakthrough.
The deepest waiting happens when God Himself seems silent.
When He gave you a promise but not a timeline.
When He showed you a glimpse of your future but left you standing in a present that looks nothing like it.
When every prayer feels unanswered.
When every dream feels delayed.
When everyone else appears to be moving forward while you remain stuck between what God said and what reality shows.
That is where Joseph lived.
And if we're honest, that is where many believers are living right now.
Joseph's story begins with a dream.
Not an ordinary dream.
A God-given dream.
Genesis tells us Joseph dreamed that his brothers would bow before him. Later he dreamed again that even the sun, moon, and stars would honor the position God had prepared for him.
The Hebrew word for dream is חֲלוֹם (chalom)—not merely imagination, but often a divinely granted revelation.
God showed Joseph something real.
The problem was that God showed him the destination without explaining the journey.
Isn't that exactly what God often does?
He reveals enough to inspire faith.
But not enough to eliminate dependence.
Joseph saw the palace.
He did not see the pit.
He saw authority.
He did not see slavery.
He saw fulfillment.
He did not see prison.
Many people assume the dream was the blessing.
It wasn't.
The dream was only the invitation.
The blessing would come through the process.
His own brothers hated him.
They stripped him.
Mocked him.
Threw him into a pit.
Then sold him for twenty pieces of silver.
Imagine the confusion.
Imagine the questions.
"God, if this dream came from You, why does my life look worse than before?"
Maybe you've asked something similar.
You prayed for restoration and things got harder.
You obeyed God and opportunities disappeared.
You stepped out in faith and found yourself facing rejection.
Joseph's story reveals a truth most Christians do not want to hear.
God's promises do not exempt us from suffering.
Very often they lead us directly into it.
But suffering is never the final chapter for those who belong to Christ.
The pit was not punishment.
It was preparation.
The slavery was not abandonment.
It was training.
The prison was not God's absence.
It was God's classroom.
Years passed.
Not weeks.
Not months.
Years.
Joseph served faithfully in Potiphar's house.
Then he was falsely accused.
Thrown into prison.
Forgotten by the very people he helped.
This may be the most painful part of Joseph's story.
Being forgotten.
Some wounds come from enemies.
Others come from people you helped.
Joseph interpreted dreams for prisoners.
One of them promised to remember him before Pharaoh.
Instead, he forgot.
Two more years passed.
Two years.
Can you imagine waking up every morning in prison knowing someone could have helped you but chose not to?
Yet even there God was working.
Genesis repeatedly says:
"The LORD was with Joseph."
The Hebrew phrase is יְהוָה הָיָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף (YHWH hayah et Yosef).
God was with him in the pit.
God was with him in slavery.
God was with him in prison.
Notice something profound.
God's presence did not remove Joseph's suffering.
God's presence sustained him through it.
Many believers mistakenly measure God's presence by comfort.
Scripture measures God's presence by faithfulness.
You can be deeply loved by God and still walk through devastating seasons.
You can be chosen and still be wounded.
You can be called and still be delayed.
Then came the moment.
The day everything changed.
Pharaoh had a dream no one could interpret.
Suddenly the cupbearer remembered Joseph.
What prison doors could not accomplish, one God-ordained moment accomplished instantly.
Joseph was brought before Pharaoh.
In a single day he went from prisoner to ruler.
From forgotten to favored.
From humiliation to honor.
From chains to authority.
The waiting was over.
But why did God wait so long?
Because God was preparing more than a position.
He was preparing a person.
A teenager with power would have been dangerous.
A mature man with humility could save nations.
The pit killed Joseph's pride.
Slavery taught Joseph service.
Prison developed Joseph's character.
The delay produced the leader the dream required.
God was never late.
God was building capacity.
This is one of the great themes of Scripture.
God prepares before He promotes.
David was anointed king long before he wore a crown.
Moses spent decades in the wilderness before leading Israel.
Paul disappeared into Arabia before becoming an apostle to nations.
Even Jesus spent approximately thirty years preparing for three years of public ministry.
The kingdom often grows in hidden places.
What God develops in secret sustains what He reveals in public.
Joseph eventually stood face to face with the brothers who betrayed him.
Now he possessed the power to destroy them.
But something remarkable had happened.
The suffering had transformed him.
Instead of revenge, he offered mercy.
Instead of bitterness, he extended grace.
Instead of condemnation, he provided salvation.
Then Joseph spoke one of the most powerful statements in all Scripture:
"You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good." (Genesis 50:20)
The Hebrew word translated "intended" is חָשַׁב (chashav), carrying the idea of weaving, planning, or designing.
The same event had two intentions.
Human evil intended destruction.
God intended redemption.
This is not saying evil becomes good.
Scripture never says that.
It says God is so sovereign that He can take what was meant to destroy you and weave it into His redemptive purpose.
That truth reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Joseph points us to Christ.
Joseph was betrayed by those closest to him.
Jesus was betrayed by one of His disciples.
Joseph was sold for silver.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Joseph suffered though innocent.
Jesus suffered though sinless.
Joseph's suffering eventually saved many lives.
Jesus' suffering saves all who believe.
The Greek word Jesus used on the cross when He declared, Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai), means "It is finished," "It has been accomplished," or "The debt has been paid in full."
What looked like history's greatest scandal became history's greatest act of grace.
The cross appeared to be defeat.
It was actually victory.
The tomb appeared to be the end.
It became a beginning.
This is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps that is why God waited for Joseph.
Not merely to save Egypt.
Not merely to preserve Israel.
But to paint a picture of the Gospel itself.
A story where suffering is not wasted.
A story where betrayal is not final.
A story where delays are not denials.
A story where God remains faithful even when circumstances suggest otherwise.
Maybe you are in your pit right now.
Maybe you are in your prison season.
Maybe people forgot you.
Maybe opportunities disappeared.
Maybe prayers seem unanswered.
Maybe you are exhausted from waiting.
Hear this carefully.
The same God who was with Joseph is with you.
The same God who worked behind prison walls is working behind circumstances you cannot understand.
The same God who turned betrayal into blessing and suffering into salvation has not stopped writing your story.
Your delay is not proof that God has abandoned you.
It may be evidence that He is preparing you for something larger than you can presently carry.
Joseph waited years.
Jesus waited thirty years.
Abraham waited decades.
God is not intimidated by timelines.
He is committed to transformation.
The question is not whether God remembers you.
The question is whether you will trust Him while He is preparing you.
And perhaps that is why this article found you today.
Not by accident.
Not by coincidence.
But because someone else cared enough to share it.
You may never know whose prison season is about to become a testimony because you chose to share.
Sometimes one message can become the reminder that keeps someone from giving up.
What season are you in right now?
The pit?
The prison?
Or the palace?
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is silently fighting the same battle.
If God has used this ministry to bless you, supporting it is one practical way to help multiply its reach so more people can encounter the transforming power of the Gospel.
Because sometimes the chapter that feels most forgotten becomes the chapter God uses most powerfully.
